93d0010f0d82e9270e149a45683930c3.text: The Williams Lake Mustangs wins the mid-week home game by 4-3 against the Merrit Centennials on Tuesday, Oct. 20. The Williams Lake Mustangs narrowly beat the Merritt Centennials 4-3 in a home game on Tuesday, Oct. 20. Late in the middle frame, the Centennials answered with another goal, leaving the game tied 2-2 heading into the third. Both teams scored once in the third period, sending the game into overtime 3-3. Neither team scored in overtime, sending the game to a shootout, where the Mustangs secured a 4-3 victory. Kaelen Swanson and Braden Bolt scored the Mustang’s two second period goals before Brenden Bolt tied the game midway through the third to help send it to overtime. Logan Hauk scored the lone shootout goal, while goalie Ivan Anderson stopped all three of Merritt’s shootout attempts to secure the Mustang’s victory. Anderson finished with 42 saves on 45 shots, while Sam Saskiw stopped 44 out of 47 shots for the Centennials. The win brought Mustangs Lake to 15 points, while Centennials earned a point for the shootout loss to reach 14, according to British Columbia Hockey Conference (BCHC). The Mustangs hold 7-2-1-0 record in their inaugural BCHC season which places them 2nd in the Interior Division and 8th overall across the league. The Mustangs return to home ice oct. 30 to host the Summerland Jets, followed by the Fernie Ghostriders on Oct. 31 at Cariboo Memorial Recreation Complex.

8667ecc30386cf533a0116aafddb05f2.text: Enjoying the Williams Lake First Nation fifth annual pumpkin patch were siblings Sofie and Shane Berkelaar who were joined with their mom Tanya. Picking out pumpkin to take home from the Williams Lake First Nation pumpkin patch held Friday, Oct. 16 was 8-year-old Shane Berkelaar. Down at Byron Louie Memorial Park for Williams Lake First Nation's pumpkin patch on Friday, Oct. 16 were Crystal Wells with her daughter Harper. The fifth annual pumpkin patch by Williams Lake First Nation (WLFN) was the biggest one yet drawing hundreds of families to celebrate the fall season with games, hotdogs and a pumpkin to take home. This was the first year the event supporting social development programming was held at Byron Louie Memorial Park located south of Williams Lake in Sugar Cane. In 2025 the pumpkin patch was held outside the Thompson Rivers University campus in Williams Lake. WLFN manager of marketing and communications Brandon Hoffman said chief and council wanted to have it closer to community while within walking distance and still attracting as many visitors as possible. The three hour event also included family photos, bouncy castle and vendors selling lemonade, bannock, ribbon skirts and more. Organizations such as Knucwentwecw Society and Denisiqi Services Society provided activities and games including spooky decorated oreos and a ring toss. Several wooden photo stand-ins were specifically made for the day by WLFN member Michaela Gilbert. Hoffman confirmed this year’s pumpkin patch was the largest one drawing over 800 people, including more than 125 WLFN members. The remaining few pumpkins at the end of the night from Sugar Cane Ranch and Save-On-Foods didn’t go to waste with WLFN ensuring they all found useful homes.

The trial for Adam Troy Mann, who is accused of her murder, is underway in New Westminster Supreme Court. Adam Troy Mann, 43, is charged in connection with Dunn’s June 16, 2024 death. He has pleaded not guilty, and took the stand on Tuesday (Oct. 20) to testify in his own defence. Mann told court when he got off a bus approximately 2.4 kilometres from Dunn’s home that night, he did so because he got into a disagreement with another passenger on the bus, and that he was unfamiliar with the neighbourhood, where he testified he found a kitchen knife and cellphone lying by the road later that evening. On Wednesday (Oct. 21) in B.C. Supreme Court in New Westminster, defence lawyer Paul McMurray spoke first, urging the jury to consider that someone is presumed innocent until the Crown satisfies “beyond a reasonable doubt” they have committed the crime they are charged with. “What is beyond a reasonable doubt? It means — and again, (B.C. Supreme Court Justice David Layton) will give you instructions about this … and you should take those instructions and not what I say, but in summary, what it means is that you need to be very certain before you can find Mr. Mann guilty of the charge that’s before you,” McMurray told the jury. “You cannot decide the case based on gut feeling, on suspicion, on anything other than a dispassionate analysis of the evidence and determination of whether or not that evidence is enough to make you certain of his guilt.” McMurray focused on Wace’s initial description of Mann, noting he compared Mann to NHL hockey player Connor McDavid and YouTube personality Shane Dawson, both of whom are white, while Mann,

76b5c428ed48918548ff510f067c6a22.text: A woman in Grand Forks has sustained severe injuries after being attacked by a dog in her own yard. Owners of a dog in Grand Forks are being asked to surrender their pet after it reportedly attacked and severely injured a woman. According to Kim Godidek, she was in her own yard when a bully breed dog from a neighbouring property broke through its owner’s fence and pounced on her. She said she was knocked to the ground by the canine, which reportedly inflicted four gashes on her upper thigh and broke both bones in her wrist, according to a GoFundMe page set up for her. The GoFundMe, with a goal of raising $8,000, aims to help Godidek over the next eight weeks, as she is unable to work because of her injuries. Godidek was given emergency medical attention, following the attack, before undergoing surgery, during which a metal plate was attached to her arm to stabilize it. The City of Grand Forks posted on Facebook Monday, Oct. 19, that it was in contact with Godidek, the RCMP, and the dog owner and that it is determining next steps. On Tuesday, Oct. 20, the city updated its response: “The city has engaged with the dog owner involved in the recent dangerous dog incident and is seeking the voluntary surrender of the dog. This would allow a qualified professional to conduct the required behavioural assessment.” “If voluntary surrender cannot be achieved, the city will be required to apply for a warrant to seize the animal.” The City of Grand Forks does not have a breed-specific dangerous dog bylaw and relies on a breed-neutral approach under its Animal Control Bylaw No. 2116. However, a dog can be deemed vicious if it has attacked or bitten, attempted to attack or bite, or chased any person, animal or wildlife without provocation. \*keep the vicious dog a minimum distance of 100 metres away from an elementary school, middle school, high school, daycare facility or any public park in the control area. 5165f67a61e1b1a76734f41f93948791.text: As the B.C. election approaches, NDP Leader David Eby, right, has urged supporters of Green Party Leader Emily Lowan, centre, to vote for his party, so B.C. Conservative Lorne Doerkson, left, doesn't win. With five parties fielding incumbent candidates in the upcoming provincial election, anxiety about vote-splitting has taken on a whole new dimension. In recent years, the NDP worried most often about a third-party challenger, with viable left-wing candidates running for the B.C. Greens in many ridings. But after two years of turmoil within the B.C. Conservative Party, more challengers have popped up, including CentreBC, a moderate vehicle helmed by former Conservative Elenore Sturko, and OneBC, a far-right party led by former Conservative Dallas Brodie. According to recent polling averages compiled by 338Canada, Conservatives lead overall, 45 per cent to the NDP’s 42 per cent. The Green Party trails with nine per cent, and the combined OneBC and CentreBC support sits between two and seven per cent. For this average of several polls, 338 allows for a possible four per cent swing either way for the top two parties. These polls only tell part of the story. Forecasting which party will form government is difficult by polling just the overall vote, according to Royal Roads University political communications professor David Black. “We have 93 mini-elections that generate this complex outcome we call government,” he said. Mario Canseco of the polling firm Research Co. points out that none of the smaller parties are running in every riding, either, which makes provincial polling inaccurate because some supporters won’t be able to choose those parties on their ballots. In addition, the numbers on the back of each jersey are adorned with the silhouette of the logo’s eye.” Team-issued photos show jerseys worn by Goldeneyes players Jenn Gardiner, Sarah Nurse and Caroline “KK” Harvey, the team’s first-overall pick in the 2026 draft. “I’m thrilled to see our new jerseys. 91f1d5f562f67e8c1d6bc46318bcb6ba.text: A CMHA survey of more than 2,500 British Columbians found that 88 per cent agree a stronger mental health system means people can access help in their communities before reaching crisis, while 82 per cent agree that waiting until someone is in crisis is too late. Ahead of the B.C. provincial election, new research commissioned by the Canadian Mental Health Association, BC Division (CMHA BC) demonstrates strong public support for strengthening mental health services and investing in prevention before people reach a crisis point. And CMHA Vernon says the research reflects what staff, volunteers, and community members see every day in the North Okanagan. The survey of more than 2,500 British Columbians found that 88 per cent agree a stronger mental health system means people can access help in their communities before reaching crisis, while 82 per cent agree that waiting until someone is in crisis is too late and that investments in housing, mental health care, and community supports can prevent emergencies before they happen. “This research reinforces what community organizations have been saying for years: people want a mental health system that is accessible, proactive, and focused on prevention,” said Julia Payson, executive director of CMHA Vernon and District. “When residents consistently identify mental health and substance use as one of the most significant challenges facing their communities, governments at all levels have a responsibility to invest in solutions that work. The time to act is before a crisis occurs, not after.” The research found that mental health and substance use ranks among the top community concerns for British Columbians, with 35 per cent of respondents identifying it as one of the three biggest challenges facing their community. The issue intersects with concerns around cost of living, housing affordability, homelessness, and public safety. Likeness of John "Cheech" Garrett on T-shirt worn by Vancouver Canucks head coach Manny Malhotra pre-game Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026 at Rogers Arena in Vancouver. Hockey broadcaster John "Cheech" Garrett on video screen at the Canucks game Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026 at Rogers Arena in Vancouver. Hockey broadcaster John "Cheech" Garrett on video screen at the Canucks game Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026 at Rogers Arena in Vancouver. Hockey broadcaster John "Cheech" Garrett and family on video screen at the Canucks game Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026 at Rogers Arena in Vancouver. Beloved hockey analyst John “Cheech” Garrett was remembered and celebrated during the Vancouver Canucks game Tuesday night, Oct. 20, vs. Carolina Hurricanes. Garrett, who lived in the Boundary Park area of Surrey, stopped pucks for the Canucks and other teams during his NHL days, 1979 to 1985, before moving to the broadcast booth at Rogers Arena. Last April Garrett died suddenly, saddening fans who fondly remember his hockey knowledge, sense of humour, warm personality and love of ketchup-covered food. He was 74. “Forever a Canuck,” Garrett’s career highlights were shown on the jumbotron pre-game, before anthems were sung. “John Garrett greeted every day with an optimistic smile, always had time for an autograph, a selfie, and a story to share with his thousands of fans and friends across the hockey world,” said Al Murdoch, in-arena voice of the Canucks. Earlier, Canucks players and coaches wore fun memorial T-shirts designed with a drawing of Garrett’s famous moustache and headset on the front. “Cheech” was also subject of trivia and a “hot dog drop” during the game, won 6-3 by the defending Stanley Cup champs, previously Hartford Whalers, with whom Garrett played goal in the early 1980s. Garrett, among the most familiar voices in Canadian hockey, worked for Sportsnet until his passing.

cfbbf8b337ab5cecfd0a01b3274675fd.text: Prince George RCMP have arrested a youth following multiple break-and-enter investigations at the same pub. According to a press release, the investigations began Oct. 6, after an alarm was triggered at 2:30 a.m. at a pub located in the 200-block of Cherry Avenue. Police found a door had been forced open and suspects had entered the building. Mounties said the second break-in attempt was reported two nights later, on Oct. 8. At about 1 a.m., on Oct. 15, officers patrolling the neighbourhood noticed the pub’s exterior lights activate. Upon arriving, Mounties found three youths behind the business. Two fled, while the third remained at the scene. According to the release, after reviewing the CCTV footage from the earlier incidents, investigators determined the youth who stayed behind was likely involved in the break-ins. The youth was arrested and taken to the Prince George RCMP detachment. He was later released to a guardian and is scheduled to appear in court at a future date. “This arrest is the result of an extraordinary amount of work by our officers throughout the course of this investigation,” Cpl. Jennifer Cooper, BC RCMP spokesperson for Northern B.C., said. “Cases like this highlight the dedication, perseverance, and diligence our police officers bring to their work each day to help keep the Prince George community safe.” Police are asking anyone who can identify the two youths who fled on Oct. 15, or who has information related to these investigations, to contact the Prince George RCMP non-emergency line at 250-561-3300 or submit an anonymous tip to Northern B.C. Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477).

5a38c848a5f9b5bf79bb5b76739d9f6d.text: A Rotary Peace Pole featuring six different languages including Tsilhqot’in, Carrier, Metis, Secwepemc, English and French has been installed in Williams Lake. A dedication ceremony was held for a peace pole located in front of Williams Lake City Hall on Wednesday, Oct 21. Williams Lake is now home to a beacon of hope the Rotary Club of Williams Lake hopes will inspire people to come together and work towards a more peaceful world. A Rotary Peace Pole was recently installed in front of Williams Lake City Hall with a gathering and dedication ceremony held Wednesday, Oct. 21. The eight foot tall, four side pole has “May Peace be in our Communities” written in Tsilhqot’in, Carrier, Metis, Secwepemc, English and French, and also a Braille plaque. Following an opening prayer by William Lulua with Williams Lake First Nation and the singing and drumming of an honour song, Rotary Club of Williams Lake past president and current treasurer Amber Stratton said the pole is now part of a global family of more than 250,000 in over 180 countries around the world. “A peace pole is an internationally recognized symbol of the hopes and dreams of the entire human family,” Stratton said. “It stands as a quiet, visual reminder of our shared wish for one simple yet powerful vision, “May Peace Prevail on Earth.”” Stratton provided a brief overview of the origins of the peace pole that was born by Masahisa Goi following the devastation of World War II and droppings of atomic bombs. She said he came to believe that by speaking, acting and living in the spirit of the mantra “May Peace Prevail on Earth” we could radiate love, harmony and peace throughout all creation. “Peace poles are intended to inspire unity among people of all backgrounds and cultures, and to serve as silent and enduring mantras for peace,” Stratton said, adding Rotary Peace Poles reflect the global service organization’s commitment to peace building and conflict prevention while serving as an important reminder that

Williams Lake First Nation (WLFN) and Thompson Rivers University (TRU) signed an Yerí7 me7 sucwentwécw-kt, an agreement aimed at improving educational outcomes for T’exelcemc students. The new agreement was signed on Tuesday, Oct. 20, and outlines how the two parties will work together on academic programs, research and shared decisions, while acknowledging T’exelc’s inherent rights, jurisdiction, and cultural authority within its traditional territory. In an Oct. 22 release on TRU’s website, WLFN Chief Willie Sellars said, “We take great pride in building relationships and partnerships with institutions like Thompson Rivers University, operating within T’exelcemc territory and lifting up both Indigenous and non-Indigenous people across our region.” Sellars further added these partnerships create meaningful opportunities to advance reconciliation, and education is a key part of that work. He said, “By supporting learning, sharing knowledge and creating opportunities for people to better understand one another, we can help build a stronger future for everyone in our region.” The new agreement includes a joint implementation plan to put the new formalized agreement into practice. Dr. Airini, TRU president and vice-chancellor, while expressing gratitude for working together as partners with T’exelc, said, “*Yerí7 me7 sucwentwécw-kt, We will recognize one another* reflects our shared commitment to creating meaningful opportunities through education and research.” She said, “We recognize the importance of T’exelcemc knowledge, language and leadership in shaping how we work together. 3e140a3cef6fa5ff5c1ba09e11d4d83c.text: Riley Windeler holds a copy of his recently published children's book Tommy’s Race at Riverside Park in Kamloops. It has been ten years in the making for Riley Windeler who has finally released his first children’s book that he hopes empowers kids in the Cariboo and beyond. The debut author who was born and raised in Horsefly but currently resides in Kamloops has a form of short-limbed dwarfism called Hypochondroplasia. Despite his small stature of four feet and six inches Windeler hasn’t let that stand in the way, serving as inspiration for *Tommy’s Race.* He received a copy of his long awaited work that is illustrated by Nora Kelly of Montreal, Que. from Caitlin Press late last month. “It has been a whole process,” Windeler said of his long awaited book. “Now it’s here and now it’s done.” *Tommy’s Race* is based off of a race from Windeler’s childhood in the small rural community east of Williams Lake. He clearly remembers the end of his first school sports day when he was about six-years-old and his friends crossed the finish line completing the race while he was still half down the field. “That was the first real time it hit me that Ok there’s this difference here,” Windeler said. *Tommy’s Race* begins with a young character named Tommy participating in a similar such race and despite coming in last place later going to a World Dwarf Athletic event after months of training to compete on a level playing field, making friends and having the courage to win. “It’s showing that yes there are these challenges but there’s also opportunities out there between the two,” Windeler said, smiling. Windeler himself persevered while he was younger playing hockey and baseball. While he said he knows he might not have been the best player he remained passionate about the sport and enjoyed playing, being awarded the most inspirational and most dedicated player by the Williams Lake Minor Hockey Association. Lucas Raymond scored twice and assisted on another, leading the visiting Detroit Red Wings to a 5-2 win over the struggling Vancouver Canucks in NHL action Thursday at Rogers Arena. William Wallinder, Emmitt Finnie and Surrey’s Michael Rasmussen also scored for Detroit (4-3-3), with Michael Brandsegg-Nygard adding two assists. John Gibson made four saves to pick up the netminding win. He left with an injury after two periods and was relieved by Michal Postava, who stopped seven of eight shots. Centre Elias Pettersson and Jonathan Lekkerimaki scored for the Canucks (2-9-1), who have dropped nine straight games. Kevin Lankinen took the loss in goal, stopping 25 of 30 shots. Raymond opened the scoring 4:18 into the first period, tipping in a point shot from Albert Johansson. Less than two minutes later, Wallinder upped the Detroit lead to 2-0, scoring from a sharp angle to the right of Lankinen. Wallinder now has two goals on the season. Pettersson cut the lead in half on the power play at 7:02, ripping a one-timer past Gibson off a feed from Filip Hronek. Pettersson has four goals on the year, all with the man advantage. Raymond countered with his second of the night and third of the year on a Detroit power play at 8:56, poking home a loose puck in the crease. Rasmussen tallied his first of the year, making it 4-1, 14:56 into the second period off another tip in of a point shot, this time from Anton Johansson. Shots after 40 minutes were 24-5 Detroit, with the Canucks failing to record a shot on goal in the middle frame. Postava, playing in his first NHL game, took over in goal for the Wings to start the third period. Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson (left) and B.C. NDP leader David Eby on the campaign trail ahead of the provincial election Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026. The B.C. Conservatives have maintained their lead in the polls three days ahead of the B.C. provincial election, but the B.C. NDP remain within striking distance according to the latest surveys. Recent polls from Angus Reid Institute and Mainstreet Research indicate the Conservatives are ahead of the NDP by three or six percentage points, respectively. The Angus Reid poll had a margin of error of three points, putting the Conservatives anywhere from 43 to 49 per cent support and the NDP in the range of 40 to 46 per cent support. Philippe Fournier, creator of 338Canada, launched the polling aggregator in 2017. He’s used it to track the last three B.C. elections, though he’s also closely followed earlier ones. Fournier told Black Press Thursday that B.C. elections rarely result in the kinds of blowouts that former NDP Premier John Horgan enjoyed over Andrew Wilkinson’s Liberals in 2020. He pointed out that in 2024, David Eby’s NDP won the popular vote only by about two percentage points, and won 47 seats — the exact threshold for a majority. “It would not take much for the NDP to drop a few points and then lose the election outright,” the polling analyst said. “Right now the polls pretty unanimously have the Conservatives ahead, although the margins vary from one pollster to the other,” Fournier added. Fournier said the polls suggest the NDP will need a strong push in the final days to retain office. “If the Conservatives match their polls and the NDP doesn’t over-perform, we’re looking at a Conservative government in B.C. 1cfff63b42dd7e57e7472e4b663031e9.text: On Oct. 20, 2026, 13 peace officers were welcomed into the RCMP's new Experienced Peace Officer (ExPO) program at BC RCMP headquarters in Surrey. A brand-new RCMP program to fast-track experienced peace officers into frontline police officers has begun, and the first troop of cadets will be training in Chilliwack. B.C. and Yukon RCMP held a ceremony at the BC RCMP headquarters in Surrey where they welcomed 13 peace officers on Oct. 20 into its new Experienced Peace Officer (ExPO) program. The 13 cadets have joined the RCMP from B.C., Yukon and Ontario and bring previous experience from various provincial, territorial and federal agencies, such as Corrections, Conservation, and Commercial Vehicle Safety and Enforcement (CVSE). They will now begin their RCMP careers through an accelerated cadet training program at the Pacific Region Training Centre in Chilliwack, which starts in November. They graduate in March 2027 and members will then be placed into frontline positions throughout B.C. and the Yukon. Assistant commissioner John Brewer, acting commanding officer of the BC RCMP, said it is a “significant milestone” and a moment worth celebrating. “Experienced peace officers bring with them a wealth of knowledge and practical experience that will make an impact in our organization,” Brewer said. The 3.5-month long ExPO training is nearly half the length of the standard six-month RCMP Depot training, which is only offered in Saskatchewan. The ExPO program was launched by BC and Yukon RCMP in July, and it is scheduled to expand to other provinces and territories in the coming months. RCMP said it recognizes the knowledge, skill and value experienced peace officers bring from previous work in the law enforcement community, and added that “by welcoming peace officers from a variety of backgrounds, the RCMP is strengthening its team while also creating an exciting option for experienced peace officers” to move forward with a career in policing. “The ExPO program reflects

ce0d1981110df369e51706c932da6fbb.text: The Veterans Review and Appeal Board upheld a 2019 Veterans Affairs decision to deny disability benefits to a 50-year-old RCMP officer after a severe abdominal injury required surgery. The officer, who is not named, had been on the force since 2008. While working in 2016 as a general duty officer for the Quesnel RCMP, the officer suffered severe abdominal pain and distention to the point that he could not put his duty belt back on. He began to feel a fever, chills and severe pain. His family doctor referred him to a surgeon. A CT scan showed a perforation in the large intestine and he underwent two emergency surgeries, used a colostomy bag for four months and had colostomy reversal surgery. “Currently on gradual return to work plan for work with limited hours. Possible hernia will always be a concern if/when I return to full duty,” said his submission. He was diagnosed with Perforated Diverticulosis, but Veterans Affairs Canada found it was not directly related to his work. In the July appeal decision, published in October, the board agreed that physical activity and compressive clothing or gear caused him pain an discomfort. “However, regrettably, the panel is unable to conclude that the applicant’s claimed condition of Perforated Diverticulosis arose out of, is directly related to or is aggravated by his service in the RCMP,” said the decision. **Election** **Conservatives remain ahead in polls as B.C. election day nears**](https://wltribune.com/2026/10/22/conservatives-remain-ahead-in-polls-as-b-c-election-day-nears/)

57a77d2b6ca0404caf3fcc3e79ad871e.text: Quesnel RCMP are asking for witnesses and dashcam footage following a fatal pedestrian hit-and-run near Yellow Marker earlier this month. According to an RCMP press release, the incident occurred shortly before 3 a.m. on Oct. 5, when officers were called to Highway 97 south after a report of a man sitting on the side of the road. Mounties said the man was located and taken to the hospital with what initially appeared to be minor injuries. According to police, the man later died in the hospital from injuries sustained in what was determined to be a hit-and-run incident. Following an investigation, police determined the man had been struck by a red 2023 Volvo tractor-trailer. Mounties have since located the vehicle and identified its driver. “Our thoughts are with the family and friends of the victim during this distressing time,” Cpl. Jennifer Cooper, BC RCMP spokesperson for Northern B.C., said in the release. “What police officers are requesting is for any witnesses or anyone with dash camera footage that captures the incident to please come forward and provide their information.” Mounties said investigators are particularly seeking footage from vehicles travelling along Highway 97 south near Yellow Market between 2 a.m. and 3 a.m. on Oct. 5. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Quesnel RCMP non-emergency line at 250-992-9211.

Conservative Party of BC leader Lorne Doerkson speaks at Taj Park Convention Centre in Surrey on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. B.C. political party leaders remain laser-focused on Surrey in days leading up to Saturday’s provincial election. Clearly the city is a key battleground for votes as candidates promise to make major projects happen in Surrey, if elected. Thursday (Oct. 22), Conservative Party of BC leader Lorne Doerkson hyped the party’s Surrey Success Plan, focused on health care, transit and transportation, to recognize Surrey’s “rightful status as the economic powerhouse it is and should be.” Meanwhile, BC NDP supporters and candidates rallied around Eby at Surrey City Hall on Wednesday evening (Oct. 21), and Doerkson plans to lead a Conservative rally in Newton on Thursday. CentreBC leader Elenore Sturko, running in Surrey South, has also focused on Surrey with platform announcements. The Conservatives say they’ll build a new women’s and children’s hospital in Surrey and also extend SkyTrain to Newton, among other election promises. Doerkson talked about his Surrey roots during a morning press conference at Taj Park Convention Centre in Newton, where many of Surrey’s Conservative candidates gathered but weren’t invited to the podium for a group photo-op with the party leader. “Surrey, of course, is always going to have a special place in my heart,” said Doerkson, schooled at Bridgeview Elementary. “I grew up here and some of my earliest memories are from childhood here.… The population has doubled in the past 25 years and is growing by approximately a thousand people every single month, which is just staggering.” Under NDP rule, he said, Surrey’s infrastructure has not kept up with growth. “Schools are crowded, emergency rooms and maternity wards are constantly closed and nobody can find a family doctor here, like the rest of the province. 5822afe96735552b2f3759df5c2f1bdb.text: ​Billie Christiansen, the founder of the Little Kitchen Company, will be featured on an upcoming episode of Dragons’ Den, a reality TV series where entrepreneurs pitch their business ideas and inventions to a panel of venture capitalists in hopes of securing financial investment and mentorship. ​Christiansen tells Black Press Media her latest creation is built around demand-driven innovation by developing original and practical products that solve frustrations that arise in the kitchen. ​“Rather than simply introducing variations of existing products, my focus is on creating genuinely innovative kitchen tools with thoughtful engineering, premium materials and distinctive designs. That commitment to innovation has resulted in 13 patents worldwide: one granted and 12 pending,” said Christiansen. ​Her latest invention, called the Twist, is a stainless steel chicken shredder and, according to her, is the only one in the world. ​Christiansen can’t give away what happens on the show, but she said it was a nerve-racking experience. ​The local entrepreneur uses software to identify high consumer demand for products that don’t exist. ​“From there, I essentially reverse-engineer the product development process, design it, create prototypes, patent it, manufacture it and bring it to market,” she explained. ​Christiansen claims her first invention, a stainless steel meat chopper, was No. 1 on Amazon New Releases for 90 straight days. ​Those who love cooking and puttering around the kitchen can catch Christiansen on Dragons’ Den when episode nine of season 21 airs on Thursday, Nov. 12, on CBC. **Election** **Conservatives remain ahead in polls as B.C. election day nears**](https://wltribune.com/2026/10/22/conservatives-remain-ahead-in-polls-as-b-c-election-day-nears/)
